ratings.plot: The allure of stardom on the big screen proves to be a road to some very dark places for Mia Goth’s titular PEARL in this stylish and gruesome prequel to Ti West’s X. With her husband away at war, Pearl finds herself dreaming of a way to escape from her boring life on the farm. She sees the silver screen as her way to find stardom and the love she so desperately needs, but her overbearing mother and her own dark impulses might hold her back from the fame she craves. PEARL proves to be a delightfully perverse study on a standout character from writer/director Ti West’s tribute to ‘70s grindhouse, X. Its vibrant, candy-coated veneer plays wonderfully against the depraved desires of the main character bubbling just below the surface. Co-writer/star Mia Goth gives another deliciously unhinged performance as Pearl, a not-quite-innocent farm girl looking for love in all the wrong places. As much a love letter to the Golden Age of Hollywood as it is a demented look at the darkness bubbling just below the surface of rural America, PEARL is colorful, unnerving, and twisted in all the right ways.

verdict.reason: Ti West's prequel is a stylish, unhinged descent into obsession and rage. Mia Goth's performance and the film's candy-colored dread make it essential theater.

ratings.plot: At Chester’s cottage, good behavior earns karaoke. Getting answers is a little more complicated. After a mysterious apocalyptic(ish) attack leaves them bloodied, disoriented, and unable to speak, Liam (Joey Bader) and Mel (Kaylee McGregor) take refuge in the English countryside. Their oddball host, Chester (Oliver Woolf), feeds them, helps them recover, and introduces a system of rewards: behave yourself, earn “nifties,” cash them in for hot-tub time and dance parties. Beyond the cottage, things are less nifty. But within it, a makeshift family is taking shape. While Liam embraces their new life, Mel grows increasingly curious about the world Chester insists is too dangerous to enter… In their feature debut, directors Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson mix deadpan comedy, sibling rivalry, and creeping unease in a coming-of-age story about people who have to grow up all over again. Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 2026 Manchester Film Festival and the Narrative Feature Audience Award at Dances With Films LA 2026, this has the sort of sensibilities that fans of Yorgos Lanthimos and Ben Wheatley will adore… and it’s a natural fit as an Alamo Exclusive.

verdict.reason: Feature debut mixing deadpan comedy and creeping unease with real formal ambition. Alamo Exclusive screened early—catch it before word spreads and the midnight crowds arrive.

ratings.plot: Where would we be without PSYCHO? Sixty years on and Hitchcock’s delicious cod-Freudian nightmare about a platinum-blonde embezzler (Janet Leigh) who neglected to consult a guide before selecting her motel still has much to answer for. It blazed a bloody trail for the much-loved slasher cycle, but it also assured us that a B-movie could be A-grade in quality and innovation. It dared to suggest that your star didn’t need to surface from an ordeal smelling of roses (or, indeed, at all). It combined a knife, a scream, a melon, some chocolate sauce, Bernard Herrmann’s greatest score, and more than 70 edits to push the envelope of screen violence. It lent The Simpsons some of its best gags. It offers perfect case studies of suspense, paranoia, and montage for lazy film studies tutors. And, of course, it was the first movie to show a toilet flushing, so we might also credit it with spawning the entire gross-out genre. PSYCHO: We salute you. (David Jenkins, Time Out )

verdict.reason: See Hitchcock's masterpiece on the big screen at no cost; a rare gift. The 70+ cuts in that shower scene still reshape how violence reads in cinema.

ratings.plot: On October 20, 1967, Roger Patterson captured 59 seconds of film showing a creature walking through the Northern California woods — footage that became the most analyzed and debated in history.
